preamble: The shift from 'ts' to 'ch' (tʃ) is a classic example of palatalization, where an alveolar affricate moves to a post-alveolar position, often triggered by following high vowels or palatal glides. However, the specific shift from [ts] to [tʃ] as a general phenomenon is not universally attested as described in the examples below.

examples.note: Development of Slavic affricates before high vowels. (This specific 'ts' to 'tʃ' shift is unattested as a general phenomenon.)
Historical development in various Romance dialects before high vowels. (This specific 'ts' to 'tʃ' shift is unattested as a general phenomenon.)

languageExamples.language: Proto-Muskogean to Eastern Muskogean (Alabama, Koasati, Creek, Mikasuki)

examples.to: Alabama and Koasati chinto, Creek cetto [tʃittoː], Mikasuki činti [tʃ]
examples.note: Follows Booker's reconstruction of *¢ [ts]; Haas reconstructed *c for this set, under which the eastern affricate would be the retention (Martin 2001). Western Choctaw sinti shows the opposite outcome *¢ > s.

examples.to: Alabama and Koasati nochi, Creek nucetv [notʃita]
Alabama and Koasati chakki, Creek cakketv
examples.note: Compare Choctaw and Chickasaw sakki. Before a consonant Alabama and Koasati show s instead (*ko¢tini 'wise' > kostini, *i¢katini 'small' > iskani), while Mikasuki keeps ičkani.
